1 Summary

About this paper. The text, analysis, figures and simulations were written by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, at the direction of Robert Drzyzgula, who set its scope and questions. It is a companion to Speed Control of Universal Motors in Sewing Machines (cited here as “the speed-control paper”), which covers the physics of the series motor and each method of controlling it. This paper looks inside the motors themselves. The sources are listed in the last section; please report errors as issues on the project’s GitHub repository.

Research use only: not a safe, buildable design. The motor-control circuits, schematics, enclosures, mechanisms, test procedures and software in this project have not been safety-designed, safety-validated, certified, or tested as a complete appliance. None of the controller designs should be built or connected to the mains as drawn, and none should be operated. A concept drawing, simulation, component listing, historical example or commercial component is not evidence of compliance or safety; printed plastic is not an assessed insulation system or fire enclosure, and a barrier drawn on a schematic is not proof of isolation. The work is meant to support understanding of how existing and historical controls work and what hazards they carry, and to guide the development of safer alternatives. It is personal learning done in public, not a product, and anyone who uses or builds on any of it does so on their own responsibility. Any future buildable design would need a new system- level engineering assessment, independent review, qualified implementation, complete-product testing and applicable certification; docs/VALIDATION.md lists what that would cover. This paper studies how the motors work; its drive options are subjects of study, not recommendations. Its curves and figures are simulations from assumed component and motor values, not measurements, and are not evidence of performance or safety.

What it covers. The speed-control paper treats the sewing-machine motor as three letters in an equation: a resistance RR, a motor constant KK, and a speed ω\omega. This paper starts from the metal and copper.

  • Construction. It shows how a universal motor is built, and which parts of it make up each term of that equation:
    • its laminated field iron and field coils;
    • its wound armature;
    • its commutator and carbon brushes.
  • Other motor types. It treats four related motors the same way, as parallel subjects rather than footnotes:
    • the wound-field DC motor, the universal motor’s DC relatives;
    • the brushed permanent-magnet DC motor;
    • the brushless DC motor;
    • the induction motor, with the industrial clutch motor and the variable-frequency drive.
    For each it covers how the motor is built, what its equations say, and how its speed is controlled.
  • Waveforms. It shows what each control method looks like on the wire:
    • the universal motor straight on the line, behind a rheostat, and chopped by a triac, where the winding’s inductance stretches and smooths the current;
    • a permanent-magnet motor on pulse-width modulation;
    • a brushless motor’s six-step drive.
  • A practical question. It closes by asking whether a DC motor exists that has a sewing motor’s power and speed, about 50–100 W at around 6,000 rpm, and also fits the space a sewing motor occupies. If so, could the MCU controller designed for the VSM Base drive it?

The short answers.

  1. The universal motor is a DC series motor built to survive AC. Its iron is laminated, its brushes are high-resistance carbon, and its field and armature share one current. That shared current is why it runs on AC at all. It is also why its speed sags under load and why its back-EMF vanishes whenever the current stops.
  2. The inductance is mostly in the field coils, and it matters. It makes the current lag the line by about 30° at full speed. Behind a triac, it carries the current past the point where the line voltage reverses. It also turns each chopped slice of voltage into a smooth hump of current. At speed the back-EMF acts like extra resistance and shortens that smoothing. At a crawl the back-EMF is gone, so the smoothing lasts longer but the torque pulses grow sharper.
  3. Permanent-magnet and brushless motors behave like voltage-controlled speed sources. Their flux is fixed by magnets, so speed follows voltage and torque follows current, each on its own. That makes them far easier to regulate, to hold still, and to brake. They need DC and, in the brushless case, an electronic commutator.
  4. The induction motor needs no commutator at all. A three-phase supply makes a field that rotates by itself, and the rotor’s bars have their currents induced by the field sweeping past. It runs at nearly fixed speed off the line, a few percent below the field, and only a variable-frequency drive changes that. The sewing trade’s clutch motor was an induction motor with the speed control in a slipping clutch.
  5. Suitable DC motors exist, and they are small and cheap. Common 24 V brushed motors of the “775” size (42 mm across) deliver 60 W or more near 7,000 rpm. Brushless motors of 42–57 mm deliver 50–100 W at 3,000–4,000 rpm. Both fit easily within the envelope of a Singer external motor. Driving one would change the controller’s power stage completely:
    • a certified 24 V supply, with no mains anywhere else;
    • an H-bridge or a three-phase bridge;
    • current sensing.
    The RP2350B, its encoder and its firmware structure would carry over. Such a controller could do what a triac never can: brake actively and hold the needle exactly where it is put.

On the simulations. The waveforms here are computed from simple lumped models with representative values for a 99-class motor, not measured. They show the shapes and the cause and effect correctly. The exact numbers belong to the motor test rig, which is designed to measure RR, LL and KK and to put these waveforms on a scope. Its captures should replace these figures.

2 The universal motor, in iron and copper

2.1 What is inside

A sewing machine’s motor, a Singer BZ or BR, or one of the generic replacements sold for them, is a small two-pole universal motor. Taken apart, it has four groups of parts.

The stator (field).

  • The iron. A stack of thin steel laminations, insulated from one another, with two inward-facing poles. It is laminated because the flux in it reverses 120 times a second on 60 Hz mains. A solid iron core would carry large eddy currents, circulating in the iron itself, and heat up (Electrical Easy).
  • The field coils. Each pole carries a coil of enameled copper wire, wound around its neck, and together the two coils make the magnetic field. On many small universal motors the two coils are connected one on each side of the armature. The motor’s circuit then runs line, field coil, brush, armature, brush, field coil, line, which keeps the armature away from both supply wires electrically and helps contain the brushes’ radio noise.

The armature (rotor).

  • The core. A laminated steel cylinder on the shaft, with slots along its length.
  • The winding. Coils of finer wire lie in the slots. Each coil’s two ends are soldered or welded to two bars of the commutator.

The commutator and brushes.

  • The commutator. A ring of copper bars on the end of the armature, insulated from one another with mica.
  • The brushes. Two blocks of carbon, each pressed against the commutator by a spring in a holder. On Singer motors the holders are reached from outside, under screw caps, because brushes wear.

The commutator is a rotary switch. As the armature turns, it keeps reversing the current in each coil just as that coil passes from under one pole to under the other. The current pattern in the armature therefore stays fixed in space, flowing one way on one side of the brush axis and the other way on the other side, while the copper moves through it. Each conductor in the field feels a force, and every force pushes the same way around the shaft.

Everything else.

  • A fan on the shaft, because more than half the input power becomes heat.
  • Two bearings. On older motors these are sleeve bearings fed by oil wicks.
  • A pulley for the belt.
  • The housing. On the 99, the motor bolts to a bracket on the back of the machine and drives the hand wheel by a belt. Others, such as the 15-91 and the 201, have a “potted” motor built into the casting.

2.2 How the parts make up the equation

The speed-control paper’s model is

v=Ri+Ldidt+Kωi,T=Ki2,v = R\,i + L\frac{di}{dt} + K\,\omega\,i, \qquad T = K\,i^2,

and each term has a physical home in the motor.

  • RR, the resistance. This is the copper of both field coils and the armature winding, plus the brushes and their contact with the commutator. Carbon brushes are deliberately resistive, because commutation on AC is harsher than on DC. The resistance limits the circulating current in the coil being switched, and so limits sparking. A sewing motor’s total is typically some tens of ohms.
  • LL, the inductance. Most of it is the field coils. They have many turns around an iron path with only a small air gap, so a modest current makes a lot of flux. The armature contributes some, partly offset by its own reaction to the field. LL appears only when the current changes, so on DC it does nothing in steady running, and on AC it is a large part of the impedance.
  • KωiK\omega i, the back-EMF. It is the voltage generated by armature conductors cutting the field. It is proportional to how fast they move (ω\omega) and to how strong the field is. In a series motor the field is made by the same current ii, so the back-EMF is proportional to both. This one fact sets the motor’s character:
    • No current, no back-EMF. When the current stops, the field collapses and the back-EMF goes with it, apart from a few volts from the iron’s residual magnetism. This is why an MCU cannot simply “listen” to a universal motor between triac pulses for its speed (§3).
    • Torque goes as i2i^2. Torque is force on conductors carrying ii in a field made by ii. When the current reverses, both the field and the armature current reverse together, so the torque keeps its direction. That is why the motor runs on AC.
  • KK, the motor constant. It folds together:
    • the number of armature conductors;
    • the number of field turns;
    • the geometry of the magnetic path.
    It is constant only while the iron is far from saturation. At high current (a stall, or a heavy start) the iron saturates, flux stops rising with current, and torque grows more slowly than i2i^2.

2.3 One constant here, two later

Every brushed motor obeys the same two laws, whatever makes its field.

  • Back-EMF: e=kΦωe = k\,\Phi\,\omega.
  • Torque: T=kΦiT = k\,\Phi\,i.

Here Φ\Phi is the field’s flux, ii the armature current, and kk a number fixed by how the armature is wound. The same kΦk\Phi appears in both, because they are two views of one exchange of energy. The electrical power the back-EMF absorbs, eie\,i, is the mechanical power the shaft delivers, TωT\omega. Both come to kΦωik\Phi\,\omega\,i.

Motors with a fixed field, shunt-wound (§4) and permanent-magnet (§5), have a constant Φ\Phi. Their kΦk\Phi is then one fixed number, and it is written twice, by the job it is doing:

  • KeK_e, the back-EMF constant, in volts per rad/s: e=Keωe = K_e\,\omega.
  • KtK_t, the torque constant, in N·m per ampere: T=KtiT = K_t\,i.

In SI units the two are the same number. Datasheets often quote them in different units, such as volts per 1,000 rpm and ounce-inches per ampere, which hides that they are equal.

A series motor has no fixed field. Its flux is made by the armature current itself, so kΦk\Phi is proportional to ii. Writing kΦ=Kik\Phi = K\,i gives the paper’s model:

  • Back-EMF: e=(Ki)ω=Kωie = (K\,i)\,\omega = K\,\omega\,i.
  • Torque: T=(Ki)i=Ki2T = (K\,i)\,i = K\,i^2.

So the single KK used through §2 and §3 is not a third kind of constant. KiK\,i is the series motor’s KeK_e and KtK_t at once, a value that rises and falls with the current. KK itself has units of volts per (ampere × rad/s), which reduce to henries. The representative motor’s KK is 0.1037 H. At its running current of about 1 A, that makes an effective Ke=Kt≈0.10K_e = K_t \approx 0.10 V per rad/s (or N·m per ampere), comparable to a fixed-field motor’s constant. From §4 on, the motors have fixed fields, and the paper uses KeK_e and KtK_t.

2.4 Why it runs slower on AC than on DC

On DC, only RR and the back-EMF oppose the supply. On AC the inductance adds a reactance X=2πfLX = 2\pi f L, which is about 57 Ω at 60 Hz for the representative 0.15 H used in this paper. It uses up part of the supply voltage without doing work. A universal motor therefore runs noticeably faster on DC of the same voltage than on AC (Electrical Easy). This is also why a DC drive such as the KBIC, which rectifies the line, drives a universal motor as a DC series motor (speed-control paper, §8).

2.5 What the nameplates say

Sewing-motor nameplates are approximate, but they agree on the scale:

  • Current: 0.3–0.6 A on 220–240 V, or about 1 A on 120 V.
  • Speed: 5,500–7,000 rpm with no load.
  • Power: outputs of roughly 25–75 W, labeled 1/15 to 1/10 hp, from about 100 W in.
  • Efficiency: about 30–40% by one collector’s arithmetic (Vintage Sewing Machines blog).

The motor on the bench here draws about 1.3 A (speed-control paper, §11). The representative motor used in the simulations below runs at about 7,000 rpm and draws 1.0 A from 120 V, and it delivers a mean torque of about 0.10 N·m, about 76 W.

3 The universal motor on the wire

This section shows what a scope would see at the motor’s terminals, and in its current, under each kind of control. The plots are computed with the model of §2, using the representative values listed with the figures: RR = 30 Ω, LL = 0.15 H, KK = 0.104 H, and a load that rises with speed. They come from tools/make_motor_waveforms.py. On the test rig, the same traces are taken with the scope behind an isolation transformer, voltage across the motor’s terminals and current across a small shunt (rig guide, §7).

3.1 Straight on the line

Three things show here:

  • The current lags the voltage. At full speed the back-EMF behaves like extra resistance, KωK\omega, in series with RR. That gives an effective resistance of about 106 Ω against the inductance’s 57 Ω of reactance, so the current lags by arctan(57/106)≈28°\arctan(57/106) \approx 28°. The power factor is about 0.88. The supply’s volt-amperes exceed its watts by that much, and a plug-in power meter shows both.
  • The torque pulses. The armature is pushed in 120 Hz bursts, hardest at the current’s peaks, with nothing at each zero. At full speed the armature’s inertia and the machine’s flywheel average this out, and all that remains is a hum at 120 Hz.
  • The current is almost a sine. The line is a sine, and the motor at steady speed is close to a fixed impedance, so the current is too. Its small distortion comes from the iron’s saturation, which the model leaves out.

3.2 Behind a rheostat or carbon pile

A series resistance leaves every waveform a sine; it only makes them smaller. The motor sees a reduced sinusoidal voltage, and the current lags it a little less, because the circuit is now more resistive. What the scope does not show is the cost. At this setting the pedal dissipates about 42 W as heat in the foot control, more than the 28 W or so that the motor delivers. That is the heat the speed-control paper describes in §3. It also explains the carbon pile in that paper’s §11, which grew hot when held just short of starting. With the motor stalled there is no back-EMF, so most of the power goes into the pile.

3.3 Chopped by a triac

How a triac switches. (The companion paper Inside a Switching Circuit covers the devices themselves.) A triac is a pair of thyristors (SCRs) back to back in one package, so it conducts in either direction. Its gate can turn it on but cannot turn it off. A short pulse of gate current starts it conducting. Once the load current has passed the triac’s latching current, it holds itself on and the gate has no further say. It turns off only when the current through it falls below its holding current, a few milliamps. In practice that means when the load current crosses zero, and then it waits for the next gate pulse. So the only control a triac offers is when to switch on in each half-cycle. This is leading-edge (forward-phase) control:

  • The line crosses zero. The triac is off, and stays off.
  • The firing angle α\alpha. The gate is pulsed, and the triac switches the full line on. α\alpha is measured from the voltage zero, so a larger α\alpha means a later start and less power.
  • The current reaches zero. The triac turns itself off.

The other scheme, trailing-edge (reverse-phase) control, switches on at the zero and cuts off part-way through. It needs a switch that its gate can turn off, a MOSFET or an IGBT, and it is what some dimmers for LED lamps use. It suits a motor badly: cutting the current off sharply in an inductive load makes the inductance answer with a voltage spike (v=Ldi/dtv = L\,di/dt). This is why dimmers sold for motors and transformers are leading-edge.

The triac switches the full line on at the firing angle and leaves it on until the current falls to zero. The plots show what the inductance does with that.

  • The voltage is a sliced sine. Before firing, the motor sees almost nothing. The line is held off by the triac, and the motor’s own terminals show only a few volts of residual-field back-EMF. At α\alpha the motor snaps to the line voltage and follows it.
  • The current is a smooth hump, not a slice. A resistor would draw a current shaped exactly like the voltage: a vertical step at α\alpha, then a sine segment ending at the zero (the dashed trace). The motor’s inductance forbids the step. The current must start from zero and rise at a rate set by LL, so it builds gradually after firing.
  • The current outlasts the voltage. Once the line passes its peak and starts falling, the inductance keeps the current flowing. That stored energy drives the current on past the voltage zero, into the start of the next half-cycle. For a short time the motor’s voltage is negative while its current is still positive, and the motor returns some of its stored magnetic energy to the line. Only when the current reaches zero does the triac turn off. This is the “conduction stretched past the voltage zero” that the speed-control paper mentions in §5.
  • Speed changes how much the current is smoothed. At high speed the back-EMF adds about 76 Ω of effective resistance. The current’s time constant is then L/(R+Kω)≈1.4L/(R + K\omega) \approx 1.4 ms, short against the 8.3 ms half-cycle, and the current follows the chopped voltage fairly closely (top panel). At a crawl the back-EMF has almost gone, and the time constant approaches L/R=5L/R = 5 ms. Each pulse then becomes a slow, rounded hump that rises late and decays late (bottom panel).
  • At low speed the torque comes in pulses. At 120° the motor gets a short hump of current twice per cycle and nothing between. Each hump gives a squared kick of torque. With the inertia of a sewing machine, this representative motor still turns at about 970 rpm. Five degrees later it is down to about 450 rpm, and by 135° this load stalls it outright. The narrow band between running and stalling is the “cogging” region of the speed-control paper, §5. It is also why an open-loop triac pedal is twitchy at the bottom of its travel.

Two practical consequences for the MCU controller:

  • The triac must be fired with a pulse long enough to latch. At large firing angles the current rises slowly from zero. If the gate pulse ends before the current exceeds the triac’s latching current, the triac drops out and the half-cycle is lost. AN1662 uses a gate pulse of about 100 µs for this reason, and so does the concept circuit.
  • Back-EMF between pulses is tiny. While the triac is off there is no current, so there is no field and almost no back-EMF. A universal motor cannot simply be listened to for its speed, as a permanent-magnet motor can (§5). This is why the concept controller uses a hand-wheel sensor.

What else the scope shows. The model leaves out two effects that a real trace has:

  • Commutation spikes. Each time a brush leaves a commutator bar, the coil it was shorting is opened with current in it. This makes small sharp spikes on the voltage, and the radio noise that the split field coils and the controller’s snubber help contain.
  • A slower start. A real triac fires only once its gate current is enough. Near α\alpha = 180° it may not fire at all, and the motor simply stops.

4 Wound-field DC motors: the universal motor’s relatives

A universal motor is one member of a family. Every brushed motor with a wound field is built from the same parts: field iron and coils, a slotted armature, a commutator and brushes. They differ in how the field coil is connected to the armature, and that one choice sets the speed–torque character. Before permanent magnets became strong and cheap, these were the DC motors, and they still drive treadmills, cranes and machine tools.

  • Series-wound. The field in series with the armature, carrying the same current. Many turns of heavy wire, because the field carries the full load current. This is the universal motor’s connection. Its torque goes as i2i^2, its speed falls steeply with load, and it races when unloaded. On DC, a series motor with no load can over-speed until it damages itself, which is why large ones are never run without a load.
  • Shunt-wound. The field across the supply, in parallel with the armature, with many turns of fine wire carrying a small, steady current. The flux is then nearly constant whatever the load. Back-EMF is proportional to speed alone, e=Keωe = K_e\omega, and torque to armature current alone, T=KtiaT = K_t i_a (the two constants are explained in §2). The speed falls only by the small iaRai_a R_a drop as load rises: the “nearly constant speed” motor of machine shops.
  • Separately excited. A shunt motor whose field has its own supply. This makes two independent controls: armature voltage sets speed up to base speed, and weakening the field raises speed above it, trading torque for speed.
  • Compound. Both a series and a shunt winding, blending the series motor’s starting torque with the shunt motor’s steadier speed.

Speed control. For a shunt or separately excited motor, the controller sets the armature voltage. Industrial drives do this with a controlled rectifier, SCRs fired in phase like a triac but feeding a DC motor through a bridge. That is the KBIC’s circuit (speed-control paper, §8). Because the flux is constant, the armature voltage minus its IRIR drop is a direct measure of speed. That is why “IR compensation” regulates a shunt motor well, and a series motor only to a first approximation.

On the wire. A DC motor on a controlled rectifier sees the rectified line’s humps, with chopped leading edges. Its armature and field inductance smooth the current much as they do for the universal motor on the triac (§3). With enough inductance, the current flows continuously from one hump to the next instead of in pulses.

Why none of this is in a sewing machine.

  • The shunt field. A shunt field wound for 120 V DC is many turns of fine wire and dissipates power continuously. The motor needs a DC supply and a rectifier either way.
  • The series connection already works. The universal motor runs directly on AC, gives high torque from a standstill, and costs little. For a machine that only ever turned one way, at the speed a foot asked for, that was enough.

Permanent magnets now give the shunt motor’s constant flux with no field winding at all, and that is the next section.

5 Brushed permanent-magnet DC motors

5.1 Construction

A brushed permanent-magnet (PM) motor is a shunt motor whose field coils have been replaced by magnets.

  • The stator. A steel can that serves as the magnetic return path, with two (or four) curved magnets glued inside it: ceramic ferrite in cheap motors, neodymium in compact, powerful ones.
  • The rest. The armature, commutator and brushes are the same as in the universal motor, only smaller for the same power. The motor has nothing else.

The common “775” motor, sold for drills, pumps and robots, is a good example. It is a 42 mm can, 66.5 mm long, with a 5 mm shaft.

5.2 What the equations say

With the flux fixed,

v=Ri+Ldidt+Keω,T=Kti,v = R\,i + L\frac{di}{dt} + K_e\,\omega, \qquad T = K_t\,i,

and in SI units Kt=KeK_t = K_e (N·m per ampere equals volts per rad/s). Three consequences matter for a sewing machine:

  • Speed follows voltage; torque follows current. At steady speed, ω=(V−RT/Kt)/Ke\omega = (V - R\,T/K_t)/K_e: a straight line falling only by the resistive drop as load rises (§4, right-hand plot). A drop that is 10% of the supply voltage at full load costs about 10% of the speed. For a universal motor at a crawl it costs nearly everything.
  • Torque at zero speed is just current. A controller that sets the current sets the torque directly, at any speed including zero. That is what makes a PM motor a servo: it can push the needle through a seam at one stitch a second, or hold it still.
  • The back-EMF is always there. It is made by magnets, so it does not vanish when the current stops. Switch the drive off for a moment and the terminals show KeωK_e\omega, the speed, directly. The speed-control paper’s back-EMF sampling (its §9), weak and noisy on a universal motor, is easy and accurate on a PM motor.

They also run backward when the supply is reversed, and they act as generators when driven, which is the basis of braking.

5.3 Speed control: the chopper and the H-bridge

A PM motor needs DC, and its speed is set by the average voltage across it. A controller makes that average by pulse-width modulation (PWM): it switches the full supply on and off many thousands of times a second, and the share of time it is on, the duty cycle, sets the average.

  • The chopper. One MOSFET in series with the motor, and a diode across the motor. When the MOSFET turns off, the motor’s inductance keeps the current flowing, and it circulates through the diode. Without the diode that current would have nowhere to go, and the voltage spike would destroy the switch.
  • The H-bridge. Four switches, two on each side of the motor. Turning on opposite corners drives it one way, the other pair drives it the other, and turning on both low-side switches shorts the motor. That short is dynamic braking: the motor, now a generator, brakes itself hard on its own back-EMF. A sewing machine that must stop with the needle in the right place wants exactly this.

5.4 On the wire

The voltage at the motor is a square wave between the supply and slightly below zero (the diode’s drop). The current is what the inductance makes of it.

  • The ripple depends on how the switching period compares with L/RL/R. Here the motor’s electrical time constant is only about 0.2 ms, against a universal motor’s several milliseconds. At 20 kHz the switching period is 50 µs, short against that, so the current rises and falls only a little in each period: the ripple is about VD(1−D)/(Lf)≈1.5V D(1-D)/(L f) \approx 1.5 A.
  • At 2 kHz the ripple is ten times larger, and the current goes discontinuous. The current is zero for part of each period, which wastes heat in the copper and makes the motor sing at the switching frequency.
  • So PWM for motors runs at 20 kHz or more. That is above hearing, and with small ripple. The RP2350’s PWM slices do this with no effort.
  • Discontinuous current changes the average. While the current is zero, the terminals show the back-EMF, not 0 V, so the average voltage, and with it the speed, depends on the load. At 20 kHz the current stays continuous and the average is simply the duty cycle times the supply.

Hearing it: the cordless drill. A cordless drill whose trigger is held just short of turning the chuck often lets out a high-pitched whine. That whine is the switching frequency.

  • Where the sound comes from. Each pulse of current pulls on the windings and the iron, and they flex very slightly at the switching rate. The motor becomes a small loudspeaker playing a tone at the PWM frequency.
  • Why it is loudest at the edge of the trigger. With the rotor stopped there is no fan, gear or brush noise to cover the tone. The duty cycle is also small, so the current is discontinuous, in short pulses that start and stop sharply. That makes a harsher, louder tone than a current rippling around a steady mean.
  • Why the tool sings at all. Many cordless tools switch at a few kilohertz to around 10 kHz, where it can be heard. Slower switching wastes less power in the transistors, and the parts cost less. Tools that switch above 16–20 kHz are silent.
  • The same holds for any battery tool. A cordless router or saw, brushed or brushless, sings in the same way, since a brushless controller chops its three phases with PWM too. A corded tool on a triac control is different: its hum is at twice the line frequency (120 Hz on 60 Hz mains) and its multiples.

The tone can be measured. A spectrum-analyzer app on a phone, held near the tool, shows a sharp peak at the switching frequency. There are two cautions:

  • Harmonics. Peaks may also show at 2×, 3× and so on. A part whose force goes as the square of the current can make 2× the strongest. If the peaks are evenly spaced, the spacing is the switching frequency.
  • A changing frequency. Some cheap controllers change frequency with the trigger’s position, so the pitch moves as the trigger is squeezed.

The certain answer is a scope across the motor’s leads, which shows the frequency and the duty cycle at once, at battery voltage, which, unlike the mains, an ordinary grounded scope can probe.

Measured: a drill and an impact driver. Two DeWalt 20 V Max tools were measured this way in a quiet room, with a phone’s microphone and a spectrum-analyzer app:

  • A DCD780 drill driver, 0–600 and 0–2,000 rpm in its two gears.
  • A DCF885 impact driver, 0–2,800 rpm and 0–3,200 impacts per minute.

Both are brushed models: replacement carbon brushes are sold for both (iFixit, vhbw). Each is a PM motor on a single PWM switch, the circuit of this section. Each tool was recorded three times: the room alone, the trigger just in, and the trigger fully in.

  • The drill sings at about 3.85 kHz. With the trigger just in, the spectrum shows a sharp line there, some 20 dB above its surroundings. It has harmonics at 7.7 kHz and 15.4 kHz, twice and four times the fundamental. The third harmonic, near 11.5 kHz, is faint.
  • It never stops chopping. The line is still there with the trigger fully in, so this drill tops out short of 100% duty. It has moved down to about 3.3 kHz, so the controller changes its frequency near full power, whether by design or as a side effect of how it controls current. The drill’s two-position speed switch is mechanical, selecting first or second gear, and it changed nothing in the spectrum.
  • The impact driver shows 7.7 kHz and 15.4 kHz. These are narrow lines that hold their frequency as the trigger moves, the signature of switching. There is no clean line at 3.85 kHz, only a broad hump from 2 to 4 kHz that grows with speed, and is more likely mechanical. So either this tool switches at 7.7 kHz, or it switches at 3.85 kHz and its fundamental is lost in the hump. A scope across its motor would settle it.
  • The speed can be heard too. In the impact driver a tall, narrow line rises from about 320 Hz to 380 Hz as the trigger goes in, and the drill shows one near 320 Hz at full trigger. A line that moves with speed is most likely the motor’s own rotation, felt through any small imbalance: 320–380 turns a second is 19,000–23,000 rpm. That is a usual speed for a small brushed motor, and a planetary gearbox brings it down to the 2,000–2,800 rpm on the nameplates. Here the spectrum doubles as a tachometer.

A faint third harmonic has a likely cause. A train of pulses at duty cycle DD has harmonics whose sizes go as |sin(nπD)|/n|\sin(n\pi D)|/n. At DD near 1/3, the third falls to nothing while the second and fourth stay strong. The motor’s mechanical response and the phone’s microphone shape the levels too, so this is a likely cause, not a proof.

What it means for control. A PM motor drive usually has two loops:

  • A fast current loop. It measures the current with a shunt resistor, once per PWM period, and sets the duty cycle to hold the commanded current, which is the commanded torque.
  • A slower speed loop around it. It commands the current.

A third, position loop can sit outside both. This is how industrial servo drives are built, and an RP2350 can run all three.

6 Brushless DC motors

6.1 Construction

Turn the PM motor inside out:

  • The magnets are on the rotor. They turn with the shaft.
  • The windings are on the stator. They stay fixed and are cooled directly through the frame.
  • The commutator goes away. There are no brushes to wear, spark or shed dust. Its job, switching current between coils at the right moment, is done by a controller with transistors.

The stator is wound as three phases, usually connected in a star.

Two arrangements are common:

  • The inrunner. The rotor turns inside the stator, as drawn. It is the form of industrial motors, including the 42 mm and 57 mm motors of §9.
  • The outrunner. The rotor is a cup of magnets turning outside a stationary wound core. This is the form of drone and model-aircraft motors: more torque for their size, but an exposed rotating can.

Poles and Hall sensors. Motors usually have 4–14 magnet poles. With pp pole pairs, the current pattern must go round its cycle pp times per mechanical revolution. Three Hall-effect sensors, set 120 electrical degrees apart, divide each electrical cycle into six states, so an 8-pole motor (4 pole pairs) reports 24 distinct positions per turn. That point returns in §9.

The ratings. Brushless motors are rated by:

  • Voltage and speed, or by KVK_V, rpm per volt, which is just 1/Ke1/K_e in other units.
  • Rated torque, rated current, and a peak torque, often about three times the rated torque, available for short periods.

6.2 Driving it

A brushless motor cannot run without its controller. Connect it to a supply and it sits still. The controller’s three-phase bridge does the commutator’s work, in one of two ways.

  • Six-step (trapezoidal) drive. At any moment two of the three phases carry current, one in and one out, and the third floats. The Hall sensors say which 60° step the rotor is in, and the controller switches to the next pair as each step is reached. Speed is set by PWM on the active switches, as for a PM motor.
  • Field-oriented control (FOC). The controller drives all three phases with sinusoidal currents, placed at exactly 90 electrical degrees to the rotor’s field. That gives the most torque per ampere and almost no torque ripple. It needs the rotor’s angle continuously, from an encoder or magnetic angle sensor, or estimated from the motor’s own voltages, and more arithmetic each PWM period. A Cortex-M33 with a floating-point unit, like the RP2350’s, does it comfortably.

On the wire. In six-step drive:

  • The phase voltages are PWM-chopped blocks. Each phase is driven high for 120°, floats for 60°, driven low for 120°, then floats again. During the floating intervals the scope shows the back-EMF rising or falling through zero. Sensorless controllers watch for that zero crossing in place of Hall sensors.
  • The phase currents are rounded trapezoids. Each rises and falls at every step at a rate set by the winding’s inductance, and carries a PWM ripple like the PM motor’s.

Under FOC the currents become clean sines with a little PWM ripple.

What it gives a sewing machine. It gives everything the PM motor does:

  • torque from current at any speed;
  • active braking;
  • holding still.

On top of that it gives:

  • no brushes to wear or spark;
  • higher efficiency, so less heat;
  • quiet running at 20 kHz PWM;
  • in Hall sensors that come built in, a measure of the motor’s position.

Brushless servo motors replaced the clutch motor (§7) on industrial sewing machines for these reasons. They are typically a few hundred watts, mounted under the table, with the controller in the same housing (Leather Machine Co.).

7 Induction motors: AC with nothing to wear

The motors so far all have something that switches the current to keep the torque going one way: a commutator and brushes, or transistors. The induction motor has neither. It is the motor of fans, pumps, compressors, table saws and almost every factory floor, and on the sewing floor it was the clutch motor that the brushless servo replaced (§6).

7.1 Construction

  • The stator. Laminated iron with slots, carrying a three-phase winding. It is the same kind of stator as a brushless motor’s (§6).
  • The rotor. A squirrel cage: a laminated core with bars of aluminium or copper running through its slots, joined at each end by a ring that shorts them all together. Taken out of the iron, the bars and rings look like a hamster’s exercise wheel, hence the name.

The rotor has no magnets, no brushes, no commutator and no electrical connection of any kind. Its only wearing parts are its two bearings.

7.2 The rotating field

Three windings set 120° apart around the stator, carrying three currents 120° apart in time, make a field of constant strength that turns. Nothing moves to make it rotate. The rotation comes from the supply itself, as each phase’s current peaks in turn. The field turns at the synchronous speed

ns=120fprpm,n_s = \frac{120 f}{p} \ \text{rpm},

with ff the supply frequency and pp the number of poles. On 60 Hz a two-pole motor’s field turns at 3,600 rpm, a four-pole motor’s at 1,800, and a six-pole motor’s at 1,200.

This is what a brushless controller does with its six transistors (§6): it makes a rotating field. The difference is that the brushless controller times the field to the rotor’s position, which it reads from Hall sensors. The induction motor’s field just turns at line frequency, and the rotor follows as best it can.

7.3 Slip and torque

If the rotor turned at the synchronous speed, the field would stand still relative to the bars, nothing would be induced in them, and there would be no torque. So the rotor always runs a little slower than the field. The difference is the slip:

s=ns−nns.s = \frac{n_s - n}{n_s}.

The field sweeps past the bars at the slip speed. That induces currents in them, the shorting rings let those currents flow, and the currents in the field make torque. A larger load slows the rotor a little more, which raises the slip, the induced current and the torque, until the torque matches the load. At full load the slip is typically 2–5%, which is why a four-pole motor’s nameplate says about 1,725 rpm, not 1,800.

The curve has three landmarks:

  • Starting (locked-rotor) torque. With the rotor standing still, the slip is 100%. The rotor currents are large but lag badly, so the torque is only moderate. The current drawn is large too, typically five to seven times full-load current. That is why big induction motors dim the lights when they start.
  • Breakdown torque. The most the motor can give, typically two to three times full load. Load it beyond this and the motor slides down the curve and stalls.
  • The running region. Between full load and no load, the curve is nearly flat. The speed falls only by the slip, a few percent, so the motor behaves much like a shunt or PM motor (§4, §5). It runs at nearly the same speed whatever the load.

7.4 Single-phase motors

A single winding on single-phase AC makes a field that pulses back and forth but does not rotate. Such a motor, once turning, keeps turning in either direction, but it has no starting torque at all. The cure is a second, auxiliary winding, set 90° around the stator from the main one, with its current shifted in time:

  • Split-phase. The auxiliary winding is wound with finer wire, so its current leads the main winding’s a little.
  • Capacitor-start. A capacitor in series with the auxiliary winding shifts its current much further, for a strong start. A centrifugal switch cuts the auxiliary winding out once the motor is near speed, which is the click heard as a table saw or a bench grinder spins down.
  • Permanent split capacitor (PSC). A smaller capacitor stays in circuit all the time. It starts weakly but runs quietly, as in fans.

7.5 The clutch motor

The induction motor’s fixed speed is its strength in a factory and its weakness at a sewing machine. The industrial clutch motor works around it mechanically:

  • The motor runs all the time, at its fixed speed, commonly about 1,725 or 3,450 rpm, driving a heavy flywheel. Clutch motors are made both single-phase and three-phase.
  • The treadle works a clutch. Pressing it pushes a cork-faced clutch plate against the flywheel, and the plate drives the belt to the machine. Letting it up pulls the plate back against a brake.
  • Speed control is slip in the clutch. A skilled operator feathers it. A beginner gets a machine that lunges to full speed, and a slow, steady crawl is hard for anyone.

The motor hums and draws power all day, sewing or not. The brushless servo that replaced it (§6) is quiet, off between seams, holds a set speed, and can stop with the needle up or down. The clutch motor’s speed control was in the operator’s foot and in the cork, never in the motor.

7.6 Speed control: the variable-frequency drive

Since the speed follows the supply’s frequency, the way to change the speed is to change the frequency. That is what a variable-frequency drive (VFD) does:

  1. A rectifier turns the mains into DC.
  2. A DC bus, a bank of capacitors, smooths it.
  3. A three-phase inverter, six transistors on PWM (2–16 kHz), turns the DC back into three-phase AC at whatever frequency is wanted.

The inverter is the same three-phase bridge that drives a brushless motor (§6). The difference is in what times it. A brushless controller follows the rotor’s position. A plain VFD just generates the frequency it is told to.

  • Volts per hertz. A winding’s reactance falls with frequency, so at a lower frequency the VFD must also lower the voltage, in proportion, to keep the same flux. It holds V/fV/f constant, which keeps the curve’s shape (the gray curves in the figure). Near zero frequency the winding’s resistance takes over, and the drive adds a little voltage boost to keep the torque up.
  • On the wire. The voltage at the motor is PWM pulses at the switching frequency. The windings’ inductance smooths them, as in a PM motor on PWM (§5), so the current is nearly a sine wave at the output frequency.
  • Vector control. A drive that models the rotor’s currents, often with an encoder, can control torque directly, much as field-oriented control does for a brushless motor (§6). Such a drive can hold full torque at a standstill. Without it, an induction motor cannot hold a load still.

Why it is not the answer for the VSM Base. An induction motor of a sewing motor’s power would be larger and heavier than the brushless motors of §9 for the same output, and needs its VFD for any speed control. A three-phase motor needs a three-phase drive. The drives sold for single-phase motors are few, and a capacitor-start motor, with its centrifugal switch, does not work on one at all. The brushless motor does the same job, is smaller, and its controller already knows where the rotor is.

8 The five motors side by side

Universal (series) Wound-field DC (shunt) Brushed PM DC Brushless DC Induction (squirrel cage)
Field made by the load current a separate field winding magnets on the stator magnets on the rotor the stator winding; rotor currents induced
Commutation commutator and brushes commutator and brushes commutator and brushes transistors, from Hall sensors or an encoder none: the supply rotates the field
Runs on AC or DC, straight off the line DC (rectified mains) DC only DC, through its controller only AC, straight off the line; single-phase needs a start winding
Torque Ki2K i^2: high at a stall KtiaK_t i_a KtiK_t i KtiK_t i rises with slip; moderate at a stall
Speed with load falls steeply; races unloaded nearly constant nearly constant nearly constant nearly constant (a few % slip)
Speed control voltage: rheostat, triac, variac armature voltage (SCR drive), field weakening PWM chopper or H-bridge PWM on a three-phase bridge frequency: a VFD
Speed feedback needs a sensor; back-EMF only while current flows armature voltage minus IRIR back-EMF read directly Hall sensors or encoder, built in none needed on the line; an encoder for vector control
Braking, holding coasts; cannot hold dynamic braking dynamic braking; holds with current dynamic braking; holds with current braking through a VFD; holds only with vector control
Wear brushes, commutator brushes, commutator brushes, commutator bearings only bearings only
Electrical noise brush sparking brush sparking brush sparking, PWM PWM none on the line; PWM on a VFD
Without electronics works (with a pedal) works on DC works on DC (no speed control) does not run works, at one speed

Read across, the table says why the universal motor won the sewing machine and why it is no longer the obvious choice.

  • Why it won. It is the only one that runs straight off the wall with nothing but a pedal. It gives plenty of torque from a standstill. It was cheap to make in 1920 and still is.
  • What it costs. Speed that depends on load, no braking, no holding, and brushes. Its low-speed weakness is the subject of the speed-control paper.
  • What changed. Strong magnets, cheap power transistors and microcontrollers moved the hard part of the motor into electronics. The brushless servo motor that replaced the clutch motor on industrial machines is that change carried through. The question for the VSM Base is whether the same change fits in a domestic machine’s motor bracket.

9 Could a DC motor drive a vintage machine?

9.1 What the job asks for

The universal motors that drive these machines set the target (§2):

  • Power: an output of roughly 40–80 W.
  • Speed: about 6,000–7,000 rpm, so a running torque near 0.06–0.11 N·m.
  • Reserve torque: a good deal more for a few moments, for a heavy seam or a cold start in old oil.

The space. A Singer external motor’s body, as measured for the test rig’s cradle, is about 51 × 64 mm in section and 114 mm long. It hangs from a bracket on the back of the machine and drives the hand wheel through a belt.

Speed itself is negotiable: the belt’s ratio sets it. A motor with twice the torque at half the speed, given a motor pulley twice the size, turns the hand wheel just as well. Power is what has to match.

9.2 Candidates

All of these run on 24 V DC. The first three fit well inside the Singer motor’s envelope. The 57 mm brushless motor fits its length and its 64 mm side, but is a little wider than its 51 mm side. Specifications are as published by the sellers cited. Ratings for generic motors vary between sellers and should be checked on the bench.

Motor Type Size Ratings at 24 V Approx. price
“775” brushed motor Brushed PM 42 mm dia. × 66.5 mm, 5 mm shaft 8,300 rpm no load; 0.082 N·m and 3.5 A at 7,354 rpm (about 63 W); 0.72 N·m at a stall (RobotShop) $12
“50SRZ” brushed motor Brushed PM 50 mm dia. × about 100 mm, 6 mm shaft Sold in 2,000–8,000 rpm versions; power ratings vary by seller (eBay listing) $55
42BLS02 Brushless, 8 poles 42 mm square flange × 61 mm 4,000 rpm; 0.125 N·m and 3.3 A rated (52.5 W); 0.38 N·m peak (Robu) $25
57BLY100, with driver Brushless, 4 poles, Hall sensors 57 mm dia. × 87 mm, 8 mm shaft 3,000 rpm; 0.33 N·m and 5 A rated (103 W) (RobotShop) $77 with driver

There is also evidence from practice:

  • A Janome 415 conversion. Robert Scheibe replaced the motor of a Janome 415 with a 24 V, 50 mm brushed motor of the SRZ family (a Tsukasa TS-50SRZ-R: 5,000 rpm, 50 × 101.5 mm, rated 10.8–50.4 W). He drove it with an off-the-shelf PWM controller and an old guitar volume pedal, through a toothed belt. He reports much better control at low speed, especially when starting difficult seams (Scheibe).
  • A brushless attempt. A SimpleFOC forum thread on brushless drives for sewing machines set targets at the hand wheel of 2,000 rpm and 0.7 N·m (about 140 W), and a smooth crawl below 8 rpm with over 1 N·m. That calls for a substantial motor. The thread recommends field-oriented control with a magnetic angle sensor, and reports no finished build (SimpleFOC).
  • Industrial machines. Brushless servo motors are the standard on industrial machines (§6), but at a few hundred watts they are far too large for a domestic machine’s bracket.

So the answer to the first question is yes. Small, cheap DC motors with a sewing motor’s power exist, and they fit its space. A brushed 775 at 24 V is the simplest candidate. A 42 mm or 57 mm brushless motor is the better one.

9.3 What the controller would become

The MCU controller in the speed-control paper is built around a triac because the motor runs on mains AC. A DC motor changes its power stage completely and leaves its brain much as it is. A concept schematic of the brushed version, a 775 on an off-the-shelf H-bridge, is in the speed-control paper’s §11 (“A DC-motor variant”) and in the repository at hardware/mcu-controller-dc/.

  • The supply becomes a certified 24 V adapter. A 24 V, 5 A (120 W) supply with a safety listing does all of the isolation from the mains, inside a part that is bought, not built. The triac, the opto-triac, the zero-cross detector, the relay and the mains wiring all disappear. Every wire the builder touches is at 24 V. For a published hobby design, that may be the largest single benefit.
  • The power stage becomes a bridge.
    • For a brushed motor: an H-bridge (four MOSFETs and a gate driver, or an integrated H-bridge rated for 10 A or more).
    • For a brushless motor: a three-phase bridge (six MOSFETs and a three-phase gate-driver IC, such as one of TI’s DRV83xx family), with the motor’s three Hall sensors wired to three GPIOs.
    • Either way: a shunt resistor and amplifier measure the current into one of the RP2350B’s spare analog inputs.
  • The firmware gains a current loop. The current loop runs at the PWM rate (20 kHz or more), with the speed loop around it, and a position loop around that for needle stops. All three fit comfortably in an RP2350. The pedal, knee and heel inputs, the speed-limit knob and the stop teaching carry over unchanged.
  • Needle stops become exact. A triac controller can only cut power early and let the machine coast to its stop, learning the coast as it goes (speed-control paper, §11). A bridge can brake the motor electrically, then hold the needle where it is with current: true servo positioning.
  • The encoder may become optional. A brushless motor’s Hall sensors report 6 states per pole pair per turn, 24 per turn for the 8-pole 42BLS02. Say the motor turns three to five times per stitch, as a 6,000 rpm motor driving 1,200–2,000 stitches a minute must. That is 70–120 positions per stitch, comparable to the optical encoder’s 144. Round and V-belts slip a little, so the hand-wheel index would still be needed to re-anchor the count once a stitch, but the expensive part of the encoder would not.

9.4 What it costs

  • Authenticity. For a collector, a vintage Singer with a modern motor is a different object. A bolt-on motor on an adapter bracket, with the original motor kept, keeps the change reversible. Machines with a potted motor built into the casting (the 15-91, the 201) are out of reach.
  • Mechanics.
    • Fitting: an adapter to the machine’s motor bracket, and a pulley sized to the new motor’s speed for the machine’s belt.
    • Bench testing: the test rig’s cradle could take a 42 mm motor with a printed adapter.
  • A motor that needs its controller. The original motor runs from any pedal; a DC motor runs only from its electronics. A brushless motor does not run at all without its controller.
  • Brushes, still, for a brushed motor. A 775 costs little enough to treat as a wear part. A brushless motor has no brushes.
  • Electrical noise of a new kind. PWM at 20 kHz, with short, twisted motor leads and a filtered supply, replaces the brush hash of the universal motor.

9.5 Recommendation

A DC-motor variant of the controller is worth keeping open, in the same spirit as the parked ideas in the speed-control paper’s §11.

  1. Start on the bench, not in the machine.
    • Measure the candidate: run a 775 and a 42BLS02 from a 24 V supply with off-the-shelf drivers, and measure speed, current and torque with the rig’s Prony brake, as for the universal motor.
    • Try it on a machine: put the better one on a machine on a temporary bracket.
  2. If that goes well, design a low-voltage power stage for the RP2350B board, H-bridge first, three-phase second. Keep the triac design for machines that keep their original motors.

The two would share their sensors, their pedals and most of their firmware.
